title: Matching Headings
summary: Matching Headings is the question type most candidates dread, and for one reason: it tests whether you can spot a paragraph's main idea rather than pick out a familiar word. Master the topic-sentence habit and it becomes one of the most reliable marks on the paper.

seo.title: IELTS Matching Headings: Method & Traps | GrowQR
seo.description: Answer IELTS Matching Headings questions: find the main idea, avoid detail-trap headings and use elimination — with a worked example and method.

objectives: Identify the main idea of a paragraph rather than a supporting detail
Use the topic sentence and elimination to match headings efficiently
Recognise the two classic Matching Headings traps and avoid them
Work out why this question type is not in passage order and plan for it

blocks.html:
Matching Headings gives you a list of headings and asks you to choose the one that best fits each paragraph or section of the passage. It sounds simple. It isn't, and the reason is built into the design: there are always more headings than paragraphs. Those extra headings are distractors, written to look tempting. Some of them will describe something the paragraph mentions — just not what the paragraph is about.

That's the whole game. A heading has to capture the main idea of the paragraph, not a detail buried inside it. Candidates who scan for a matching word get pulled straight into the traps. Candidates who ask "what is this paragraph mainly doing?" get the marks.

blocks.title: This task is not in passage order
blocks.html: Unlike True/False/Not Given or sentence completion, Matching Headings answers do not follow the order of the passage. You can't assume the answer to paragraph B sits neatly after the answer to paragraph A in the list. Work paragraph by paragraph through the text, and let the heading list be a menu you keep returning to — not a sequence.

Why the main idea, not the detail?

A well-written paragraph makes one central point and supports it with examples, statistics or explanation. The examiners write one heading for that central point and other headings that echo the supporting details. Consider a paragraph whose main idea is "electric cars are still too expensive for most buyers," which happens to mention that batteries are recyclable. A heading like "Recycling and the environment" is a trap: recycling appears in the paragraph, but the paragraph isn't about it. The correct heading is the one about cost.

So your first job on every paragraph is to strip away the examples and name the one idea the whole paragraph exists to make.

The topic-sentence habit

In most academic paragraphs the main idea sits in the first or second sentence — the topic sentence — and sometimes it's restated at the end. Read the opening, form a quick sense of the point, then check the last sentence to confirm the paragraph didn't pivot. Only if those don't settle it do you weigh the middle. This isn't a shortcut that skips the paragraph; it's a way of reading it with the right question in mind.

One warning: not every paragraph is that tidy. Some bury the main idea in the middle, or build it across the whole paragraph. When the topic sentence is misleading, that's usually deliberate — read the whole thing before committing.

blocks.title: A reliable method
items: Read the paragraph fully, then say its point in your own words — one short phrase, before you look at the headings. This stops the heading list from steering you.
Find the heading that matches your phrase, not the one that shares a keyword with the paragraph.
Cross off each heading as you use it. One heading per paragraph; a used heading can't return. This shrinks the menu and makes later paragraphs easier.
Do the paragraphs you're sure of first. Skip a hard one, come back — the ones you've eliminated will narrow the choice.
For the last paragraph, use elimination. If you've matched the rest confidently, the remaining heading is often forced — but re-read to confirm it genuinely fits, not just that it's left over.
Never leave one blank. Even a best guess from the leftover headings has a real chance of being right.

blocks.title: Worked example: spot the main idea
blocks.prompt:
List of Headings

  1. The high cost of switching to solar
  2. How solar panels are manufactured
  3. Falling prices open solar to ordinary households
  4. Government subsidies for renewable energy

Paragraph A. "For decades, rooftop solar was a luxury reserved for the wealthy or the ideological. A single installation could cost as much as a small car, and payback took fifteen years. That calculation has changed. The price of photovoltaic panels has dropped by nearly 90 per cent since 2010, and installation costs have followed. Today an average suburban family can fit panels for a sum that pays for itself within six or seven years — a shift that has moved solar from the fringe into the mainstream."

Paragraph B. "Manufacturing a solar panel begins with purified silicon, which is sliced into thin wafers. These wafers are treated to create an electric field, coated with an anti-reflective layer, and wired into cells. Dozens of cells are then sealed behind tempered glass to form a single weatherproof panel capable of lasting twenty-five years or more."

Which heading fits Paragraph A, and which fits Paragraph B?
blocks.answer: Paragraph A → iii (Falling prices open solar to ordinary households). Paragraph B → ii (How solar panels are manufactured).
blocks.explain: Paragraph A mentions high cost (heading i) in its first two sentences — that's the trap. But the paragraph's whole point is that the cost has fallen and solar is now affordable for ordinary families. The main idea is the change, not the old expense, so iii is correct and i is a detail-trap. Heading iv (subsidies) is never mentioned at all. Paragraph B is a straightforward description of the manufacturing process, matching ii cleanly. Notice that once A takes iii and B takes ii, headings i and iv are the unused distractors — exactly the "more headings than paragraphs" design.

blocks.title: The two traps that catch everyone
blocks.html: Trap 1 — the detail heading. A heading names something the paragraph mentions in passing but isn't mainly about. If you match on a shared word, you'll fall for it. Trap 2 — two near-identical headings. The list will sometimes offer two headings that differ by one crucial word ("causes of" vs "effects of", "a problem" vs "a solution"). When two headings feel close, that difference is the whole question — decide which one the paragraph actually supports.

What the heading doesLikely statusYour move
Captures the paragraph's central pointCorrect answerMatch it and cross it off
Names a detail or example inside the paragraphDetail trapReject — it's not the main idea
Uses a word from the paragraph but shifts the meaningKeyword trapReject — check meaning, not vocabulary overlap
Very close to another heading, one word differentDiscriminator pairDecide which word the paragraph supports
Describes nothing in the paragraphPure distractorIgnore; it exists to pad the list

blocks.title: Read the example paragraph, if there is one
blocks.html: Sometimes the instructions match one paragraph for you as a worked example and remove its heading from the choices. Read that example — it shows you the level of "main idea" the examiners are working at, and it removes one heading from your menu. Free information; use it.

The same task in both tests

Matching Headings appears in both Academic and General Training Reading — most often on the longer, more discursive passages, which on GT means Section 3. The method is identical. The one thing that changes with practice is speed: once naming a paragraph's main idea becomes automatic, this question type stops eating your clock and starts banking marks. If it still feels slow, that's a sign you're reading for keywords rather than for the point.

faqs.q: Why are there more headings than paragraphs in IELTS Matching Headings?
faqs.a: The extra headings are deliberate distractors, several of which describe a detail that appears in a paragraph without being its main idea. They test whether you can identify the central point rather than match on a shared keyword.

faqs.q: Are Matching Headings questions in the same order as the passage?
faqs.a: No. Unlike True/False/Not Given, this question type does not follow passage order. Work through the paragraphs in turn and treat the heading list as a menu you keep returning to.

faqs.q: Should I read the whole paragraph or just the first line?
faqs.a: Read the whole paragraph, but pay special attention to the first and last sentences, where the main idea usually sits. Some paragraphs bury or delay the main point deliberately, so never decide on the opening line alone.

faqs.q: What is the most common mistake in Matching Headings?
faqs.a: Choosing a heading that matches a detail mentioned in the paragraph rather than its overall point. Always name the paragraph's main idea in your own words first, then find the heading that fits that phrase.
